docs.title: Nigerian International Passport Renewal 2026
docs.short: Renew your passport in 2026: fees, timelines, the online portal, and what to avoid.
docs.fee: ₦100,000 (32 pages, 5 years) or ₦200,000 (64 pages, 10 years) for applications within Nigeria. Diaspora fees: $150 (5-year) or $230 (10-year).
docs.feeSource: Fee increase effective 1 Sept 2025, reported again in 2026 coverage. Confirm on immigration.gov.ng before paying.
docs.timeline: Roughly 3 weeks after biometric capture for renewals; about 6 weeks for fresh applications (reported 2026 range).
steps: Create or log into your account on the NIS online portal (immigration.gov.ng).
Make sure your NIN is linked to your record, because the portal pulls details from NIMC.
Select the booklet type: 32 pages (5-year) or 64 pages (10-year).
Fill in the form exactly as it appears on your old passport and NIN slip.
Pay online. NIS does not accept cash at its offices for this service.
Book your biometric capture slot and attend with the original documents.
Track your application using the reference number. Collect or request home delivery where offered.
documents: Passport photograph in the required format
Email and phone number that you check daily
pitfalls: Paying agents who promise 'fast track' for cash
Name mismatch between your NIN and your passport
Missing the biometric appointment
Applying with a damaged photo

docs.title: NIN Correction and Modification 2026
docs.short: Fix your NIN name, date of birth, address or phone number without paying a 'agent' ₦20,000.
docs.fee: Name, address, phone or other data field: ₦2,000 per request. Date of birth: ₦28,574. NIN slip reissue: ₦600.
docs.feeSource: NIMC service charges reported as of July 2026. Some older articles say the service is free, so check before you pay.
docs.timeline: Varies by field and by NIMC office. Self-service requests are often faster than walk-in visits.
steps: Go to NIMC's official self-service modification portal (nimc.gov.ng).
Create an account with your NIN and a phone number you can access.
Select the field to correct, such as name or DOB.
Upload the supporting document in clear PDF or JPEG under 2MB.
Pay the fee through the portal's Remita payment flow.
Save your reference number and check the status regularly.
documents: Birth certificate or court affidavit (for name or DOB changes)
Debit card or mobile banking app for payment
pitfalls: Cash 'processing' from touts at NIMC gates
Fake NIMC websites that collect your details
Uploading blurry or cropped documents
Paying twice because the portal shows a timeout

docs.title: Police Character Certificate 2026 (Police Clearance)
docs.short: How to get a police character certificate in 2026: official fees, steps, and the scam signs to avoid.
docs.fee: ₦30,000 official fee through the POSSAP portal (reported 2026). Some in-person biometric stations add informal charges of ₦5,000 to ₦10,000.
docs.feeSource: Reported 2026 official fee. Check the POSSAP portal before paying, because informal charges are not official.
docs.timeline: Varies. Plan 2 to 6 weeks, and remember the certificate is commonly valid for about 3 months.
steps: Register on the POSSAP portal (Police Clearance / Character Certificate).
Fill in your personal details and upload the required documents.
Pay the official fee and keep the payment receipt.
Book your biometric capture (fingerprints and photo) at the listed centre.
Track the status on the portal and collect your certificate when it's ready.
If you need international authentication, follow the Ministry of Foreign Affairs process separately.
documents: Any supporting letters the portal asks for
pitfalls: Paying 'express' cash fees to officers
Using a fake portal link from a WhatsApp group
Forgetting the 3-month validity window
Not checking the spelling of your name on the certificate

docs.title: CAC Business Name Registration 2026
docs.short: Register your business name in 2026: exact fees, steps, and how to avoid the agent markup.
docs.fee: ₦500 name reservation plus ₦10,000 registration fee (₦10,500 in official CAC fees, per the schedule reported in 2026). Some agent sites quote ₦20,000 or more, so check the current CAC schedule.
docs.feeSource: Multiple 2026 reports. Verify on cac.gov.ng or services.cac.gov.ng before paying.
docs.timeline: About 1 week for a business name, when the application is complete.
steps: Search for your name on the CAC public search portal (publicsearch.cac.gov.ng). It's free.
Reserve the name and pay the reservation fee on the CAC portal (services.cac.gov.ng).
Complete the business name registration form with your details and address.
Pay the registration fee and keep the receipt.
Download your certificate once approved. Keep a soft and hard copy.
Get a TIN for the business from the tax authority.
documents: Two proposed business names (in order of preference)
pitfalls: Agents adding hidden charges after you pay
Choosing a name that is too close to an existing one
Forgetting the 60-day reservation window
Not keeping copies of your certificate

docs.title: Tax for Freelancers in Nigeria 2026 (TIN and Filing)
docs.short: How freelancers get a TIN, what they pay tax on in 2026, and how to stay out of trouble.
docs.fee: Getting a TIN is free through the official tax portal. Tax payable depends on your income and the reliefs you claim. Agents often charge for filing.
docs.feeSource: New tax laws took effect in 2026. Check the current rules with the tax authority or a registered tax professional.
docs.timeline: A TIN can be obtained within days. Annual filing deadlines apply.
steps: Get your TIN through the official tax portal using your NIN.
Open a separate account for business income so records are clear.
Keep invoices, bank statements and receipts for every expense.
Calculate your taxable income each quarter so you're not caught out in December.
File your returns on time through the official portal.
Ask for a tax clearance certificate when you need it for contracts or bank loans.
pitfalls: Mixing personal and business money
No invoices for foreign clients
Ignoring the filing deadline
Paying random agents for a free TIN

docs.title: Nigerian Driver's Licence: Fresh Application and Renewal (3-Year vs 5-Year)
docs.short: A fresh Nigerian driver's licence runs through a certified driving school, a VIO driving test, payment on the official portal, confirmation at your State BIR or MVAA, and biometric capture at an FRSC Drivers Licence Centre. A renewal drops the school and the test but keeps the payment and the capture.
docs.fee: ₦10,350 for three years or ₦15,450 for five years, the last FRSC-published figure we could verify. We re-read FRSC's service agreement and both official portals on 14 October 2026 and no newer published amount was there, so confirm the amount your portal payment page generates before you pay.
docs.feeSource: FRSC Service Level Agreements, Second Edition, April 2024, on frsc.gov.ng (re-read 14 October 2026). Neither frsc.gov.ng nor the licence portal's public pages published any payable licence amount on 14 October 2026, so the amount the portal itself generates is the one to pay.
docs.timeline: FRSC's published standard is a temporary licence issued on the spot at capture, valid for 60 days, with the permanent card collected from the State BIR or MVAA after 60 days. Renewal opens one calendar month before your licence expires. A licence verification extract through FRSC's own NDL portal is stated to be ready within 10 working days.
steps: Sort out your NIN first. It is the identity record the FRSC process runs on, so a mismatch between your NIN and your other documents will stall the application.
Get a learner's permit from your State Board of Internal Revenue, Motor Licensing Authority or Motor Vehicle Administration Agency.

Choose a certified driving school from the FRSC Driving School Standardisation Programme list at dssp.frsc.gov.ng, and check the grade the school holds before you pay. FRSC's service agreement puts the training at 26 sessions, followed by the school's exam and capture.
Collect your certificate of completion. The certificate number is what calls up your pre-populated record on the official portal.
Sit the VIO driving test. Pass and you get a Driver's Test Certificate. Fail and you may apply again, but not earlier than one calendar month after the failed test.
Complete the application online at the official Nigeria Driver's Licence portal and choose three years or five years.

Pay the licence fee through the portal or at a designated bank. FRSC's service agreement names FCMB, FBN, Access, UBA, Union and Sky Bank, using the PAYARENA / E-PAYMENT platform, and says to keep the teller. Pay only against a reference the system generates for you.
Take the payment to the State BIR or MVAA for confirmation. Applications regularly stall at this step.
Go to the FRSC Drivers Licence Centre for the vision acuity test, then biometric and bio-data capture.
Expect a biometric investigation on your record at the FRSC Data Centre before the permanent card is produced. FRSC's service agreement runs that check after capture at the DLC.
Collect the temporary licence, which FRSC issues on the spot with 60 days of validity.
Collect the permanent card from the State BIR or MVAA after 60 days.

Activate the eNDL digital licence in the FRSC app once your record is complete. The portal is explicit that fresh applicants must finish the full process including biometric enrolment first, and the app is Android-only at present.
documents: Driving school certificate of completion (fresh applications)
Medical certificate of fitness from a designated government hospital (commercial or professional licences)
Police extract and a sworn affidavit (reissue after loss, theft or damage)
For a foreign licence exchange: passport data page, the foreign licence, proof of residence, and a letter of authentication or driving history
Bank teller or e-payment receipt from the designated bank, kept for the BIR or MVAA confirmation
Acknowledgement slip printed from the portal after payment
pitfalls: Paying for a licence that skips capture. If nobody took your fingerprints and photo at an FRSC centre, the card will not pass FRSC verification at a checkpoint.
Starting from a link in a WhatsApp group instead of typing the portal address yourself.
Handing cash to someone at the gate instead of paying against the reference the portal generates.
Waiting until the licence has already expired. The renewal window opens one calendar month before the expiry date.
Skipping the payment confirmation at the State BIR or MVAA.

Assuming the licence fee differs by state. FRSC's own harmonisation documents say the fee is the same across the country; what differs is what a driving school charges and what state agencies charge for the permit and the test.
Letting more than six months pass after expiry. FRSC requires a fresh driving test before renewal once that much time has elapsed.
Choosing a driving school you have not checked on dssp.frsc.gov.ng. FRSC grades schools, and a school that drops below its minimum standards can have its certification suspended or withdrawn.
Trusting a 'fast track' that skips the 26 sessions. The only documented bypass we could verify is the foreign-licence reciprocity route, and that is for people who already hold a foreign licence.
Not printing the application form and the acknowledgement slip after you pay. Both are free on the portal, and you will want them at the centre.
Paying a fee that is not displayed on the portal's own payment page. A figure that only exists in somebody's message is a quote from a person, not from FRSC.
docs.metaTitle: Nigerian Driver's Licence: Fresh Application & Renewal (FRSC)
docs.metaDescription: The official FRSC route to a Nigerian driver's licence: certified driving school and its FRSC grade, VIO test, payment, BIR or MVAA confirmation and biometric capture — plus the 3-year vs 5-year choice, do-it-yourself licence verification, and how to avoid a fake no-capture card.

how to renew drivers licence nigeria

headings.cost: What it costs, and how to confirm the fee before you pay

docs.sourceNote: Everything except the fee comes from FRSC documents and FRSC-run portals, all re-read on 14 October 2026: FRSC's Service Level Agreements, Second Edition, April 2024 (fee lines, designated banks, the 26-session standard, bypass capture, the biometric investigation at the FRSC Data Centre and the NDL verification procedure); the Driving School Standardisation Programme portal at dssp.frsc.gov.ng (certification grades, curriculum, instructor certification and sanctions); the NDL verification portal at ndlverification.frsc.gov.ng (the six-step verification request and shipping flow); and the official Nigeria Driver's Licence portal at nigeriadriverslicence.org (application options, the six-step process, reissue conditions and the eNDL digital licence notice). The fee is the weakest figure on this page: ₦10,350 for three years and ₦15,450 for five years is the most recent FRSC-published amount we can read, dated April 2024, and the higher figures quoted in 2026 write-ups could not be confirmed on any FRSC page.

unverifiedItems: The current statutory licence fee. The newest FRSC-published figure we could verify is ₦10,350 for three years and ₦15,450 for five years, from FRSC's Service Level Agreements, Second Edition, April 2024. On 14 October 2026 we re-read that document and both FRSC-run portals and found no newer published amount. Start the application and pay the amount the portal generates.

The ₦15,000 (three years) and ₦21,000 (five years) figures that circulate in 2026 write-ups and are credited to the FRSC portal. We could not find either amount published anywhere on frsc.gov.ng or on the licence portal's public pages on 14 October 2026, so we are not printing them as the fee.
Driving school fees, including any charge for the school's own exam and capture. These are set by each school and are not published nationally, so get the full cost in writing before you enrol.
Learner's permit and VIO test charges. These are set by state agencies (BIR, MLA or MVAA) and differ by state.
Card collection time in your state. FRSC's standard is 60 days, but individual centres vary.
Any figure an agent or a blog quotes that is higher than the amount the portal itself generates.
extraIntro: The last licence fee FRSC has published that we could verify is ₦10,350 for a three-year licence and ₦15,450 for a five-year licence, from FRSC's Service Level Agreements, Second Edition, April 2024. Higher amounts are quoted all over the internet for 2026, but we could not confirm any of them on an FRSC page, so we have left the fee marked as unverified rather than repeat a number we cannot stand behind. The portal generates the amount you actually pay — use that.

Everything else on this page is firmer. The steps, the 60-day standard, the one-month renewal window and the driving school requirement all come from FRSC documents and the official licence portal, and we read each of them on 12 October 2026.

We went back through FRSC's service agreement and the two FRSC-run portals on 14 October 2026 to see whether anything on the fee had moved. Nothing had: no payable amount is published on the public pages we can read, so the fee stays labelled as unverified rather than replaced with a guess.

What we did find is depth. The grades a driving school is certified in, the bank-and-reference route FRSC's own service agreement describes for payment, the biometric investigation that runs at FRSC's data centre before your card is produced, and the six-step process for verifying a licence yourself are all on this page now, each traceable to an FRSC document or an FRSC-run portal.

extraSections.h2: Fresh application and renewal, side by side
paras: The two routes share the same spine: online application, payment, payment confirmation, capture, collection. What differs is everything that proves you can actually drive.

extraSections.h2: Three years or five years: how to choose
paras: FRSC's service charter sets the validity of a Nigerian driver's licence at three or five years, and both options are open to first-time applicants as well as to renewals. The fee lines for both durations appear in FRSC's new-issue procedure and in its renewal procedure.

Using the last FRSC figures we could verify, five years costs ₦5,100 more than three. In return you skip one renewal cycle: one less payment, one less trip to a capture centre, and one less chance of letting the card lapse and having to sit a driving test again.
Take the five-year option if your details are settled and you expect to keep driving. Take the three-year option if cash flow is tight right now, or if you expect to change your name or address soon.

extraSections.h2: The driving school step, and why the certificate number matters
paras: FRSC's service agreement is specific here. Pick your school from the certified list on the Driving School Standardisation Programme portal at dssp.frsc.gov.ng, complete the training, and sit the school's exam and capture.

The school then issues a certificate of completion, and that certificate number is what calls up your pre-populated record on the official portal. If a school cannot show you its certification, or offers to skip the sessions, walk away — the rest of the process will not run without that certificate.
Driving school charges are not published nationally and vary by school and by state. Ask for the full cost in writing before you enrol, and ask whether it covers the school's exam and capture.

extraSections.h2: How to avoid a fake 'no-capture' licence
paras: This is the single biggest risk on this page, and it is the reason forum threads about licences are unsafe to follow. A card printed without your biometrics ever touching an FRSC machine is not a licence. It is a piece of plastic that fails verification at a checkpoint and leaves you exposed to a fine.
bullets: Fresh applicants must complete the full process including biometric enrolment. There is no legitimate shortcut, and the official portal says so in its own digital licence notice.

Bypass capture is real, but it is a renewal-only feature. FRSC's service agreement says it is offered only on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th renewal and so on. If you answer NO, your original biometrics are reused on the renewed card.
Anyone advertising a licence 'without capture' to a first-time applicant is selling a fake.
Verify a card before you trust it. FRSC runs its own licence verification service at ndlverification.frsc.gov.ng.
Pay only against the payment reference the portal generates. Never hand cash to somebody who promises to fast-track the file.

extraSections.h2: Commercial and professional licences
paras: A commercial or professional licence has a higher bar. FRSC's service agreement requires the applicant to be 26 or older, to already hold a private licence, and to show evidence of membership of a professional association such as NURTW or NARTO, or a letter of employment from a registered transport company.

It also requires a medical certificate of fitness from a designated government hospital covering blood pressure, visual acuity and colour blindness, blood sugar for diabetes, chronic arthritis, an EEG screening for epilepsy, and ear defects. The applicant then sits a VIO driving test.

extraSections.h2: If your licence is lost, stolen or damaged
paras: That is a reissue, not a renewal, and the official portal sets out the conditions: obtain a police extract stating the particulars of the loss, damage or defacement, swear an affidavit stating the same facts, and pay the prescribed fee.
Start from the reissue option on the portal itself. Do not hand the extract and the affidavit to a third party to process on your behalf.

extraSections.h2: Exchanging a foreign licence
paras: FRSC runs a foreign driver's licence reciprocity process through its MVA department. The documents listed are the data page of your international passport, the foreign licence, proof of residence in Nigeria, and a letter of authentication or driving history from the country that issued it.
You will be referred to the State VIO for a retest, and a Driver's Test Certificate is issued if you pass.

extraSections.h2: Choosing a driving school you can actually check (and what its grade means)
paras: FRSC does more than keep a list of schools: it scores and grades them. The Driving School Standardisation Programme portal at dssp.frsc.gov.ng lets you search certified schools by state, and it publishes the grading table a school is measured against.

That matters because the certificate of completion is your entry ticket to the rest of the process. If the school is not certified, or is holding a certificate from a school whose certification was suspended, the file stops moving.

table.caption: FRSC Driving School Standardisation Programme — assessment and grading of driving schools, dssp.frsc.gov.ng, read 14 October 2026.

bullets: Instructors are trained and certified by FRSC as well, and their registration is renewed annually.

The uniform driver-education curriculum runs to 21 modules. The published course lengths are three months for the Basic Learner Driver Course, two months for the Proficiency course, and one month each for the Executive and Specialised courses.

FRSC says a proprietor who does not register is prosecuted under the FRSC Act 2007 and the National Road Traffic Regulations 2004, and that certification is suspended or withdrawn when a school drops below the standard.
Ask your school for its certification grade and its FRSC instructor details before you pay. A school that cannot answer is the wrong school.

extraSections.h2: Where the money goes: the payment route FRSC's own service agreement describes
paras: This is the step where people lose money, so it is worth being precise. FRSC's service agreement says the prescribed licence fee is paid at a designated bank — it names FCMB, FBN, Access, UBA, Union and Sky Bank — using the PAYARENA / E-PAYMENT platform, and is then confirmed at the State BIR or the Motor Vehicle Administration Agency.

The portal also takes online payment when the application is filed online, and the portal's own six-step summary places payment after the VIO test and before the BIR confirmation. Either way, the shape is the same: a reference is generated for you, the money moves against that reference, and somebody at BIR or MVAA confirms it before biometric capture.

The bank list is from FRSC's April 2024 service agreement, so read it as the documented route rather than a promise about today's counter list. The principle behind it still holds: no reference, no payment.
bullets: Never hand cash to a person who cannot show you the payment reference on the portal or on a bank teller.
Keep the teller or the e-payment receipt. The BIR or MVAA confirmation step runs on it.
If somebody quotes you a 'current' fee that the portal's payment page does not show, ask them to show you the amount on the portal. If they cannot, treat the figure as unverified.

extraSections.h2: Verifying a licence — do it yourself, from anywhere
paras: FRSC runs its own verification service at ndlverification.frsc.gov.ng. It is the same system an employer, a car-hire company or a foreign licensing authority uses, and you do not need an agent to stand in front of you while you use it.
The portal describes six steps, and FRSC's service agreement adds the document list and the turnaround.
bullets: 1. Sign up — create an account with a few details.
2. Fill the verification form — upload an application letter, the front page of the licence, the back page, and any means of ID such as a voter's card, international passport or NIN.
3. Add shipping details if you want the extract sent to you.
4. Pay — the verification fee, the shipping fee, or both, with a debit card.

5. Wait for verification — FRSC's service agreement states the extract should be ready within 10 working days, and the portal mails you progress updates through the review levels. Download the extract from the portal when it is ready.
6. Confirm delivery — if documents are shipped you get a tracking number, and you mark the request settled on the portal once it arrives.

extraSections.h2: The temporary licence, the permanent card and the eNDL digital licence
paras: After capture at the Drivers Licence Centre, FRSC runs a biometric investigation on your record at its data centre. That check sits between your temporary licence and the permanent card, and it is why a 'captured on paper only' card never survives it.

The temporary licence is printed and issued on the spot with 60 days of validity, and the permanent card is collected from the State BIR or MVAA after 60 days. FRSC's service agreement also says the reason must be communicated to you if the permanent card will not be produced inside that standard, so ask for it in writing if you are kept waiting.

The portal also carries a digital licence, the eNDL, activated through an app. Its notice on the portal is blunt: fresh applicants are required to complete the full application process including biometric enrolment before activation, and an expired licence must be renewed first. The app is Android-only at present.

extraSections.h2: The fee we still cannot confirm — and why we will not print a guess
paras: Every other rule on this page comes from a document or portal we can point at. The current statutory fee does not. The newest FRSC-published amount we can read is ₦10,350 for three years and ₦15,450 for five years, in FRSC's Service Level Agreements, Second Edition, April 2024. We re-read that document, this portal and the FRSC site on 14 October 2026 and found no newer published amount.

In the same round of checking, 2026 write-ups said the fee is now ₦15,000 for three years and ₦21,000 for five years, and credited those figures to the FRSC portal. We could not find either amount published anywhere on frsc.gov.ng or on the licence portal's public pages that day, so we are not printing them as the fee. That is not us being difficult: a figure we cannot trace is exactly the figure an agent will use against you at the gate.

What you can rely on is the process, not the rumour. Start the application in the portal, look at the amount the payment page generates, pay it against the reference it gives you, and keep the receipt. If a number does not appear on the portal's own payment page, it came from a person.

extraFaqs.q: How much is a Nigerian driver's licence right now?
extraFaqs.a: The most recent fee FRSC has published that we could verify is ₦10,350 for a three-year licence and ₦15,450 for a five-year licence, from FRSC's Service Level Agreements, Second Edition, April 2024. We could not confirm the higher figures quoted for 2026 on any FRSC page, so start the application in the portal and pay the amount it generates.

extraFaqs.q: When can I renew my licence?
extraFaqs.a: FRSC's service agreement says the holder of a valid licence may apply for renewal at any time within one calendar month before the expiry date. The official portal words it as from 30 days before expiry. Do not wait until after the card expires.

extraFaqs.q: Do I have to redo driving school when I renew?
extraFaqs.a: No. Renewal drops the learner's permit, the driving school and the VIO test. The one exception is a driving test, which FRSC requires if six months have elapsed since you last held a valid licence.

extraFaqs.q: What is bypass capture, and can I use it?
extraFaqs.a: It is a renewal-only feature that lets you reuse your existing biometrics instead of being captured again. FRSC's service agreement says it is available only on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th renewal and so on, not on every renewal. Fresh applicants cannot use it.

extraFaqs.q: How do I check whether a licence is genuine?
extraFaqs.a: Use FRSC's own licence verification service at ndlverification.frsc.gov.ng. A card produced without biometric capture at an FRSC centre will not verify.

extraFaqs.q: Can a first-time applicant get the five-year licence?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. The fee lines for both the three-year and the five-year validity appear in FRSC's new-issue procedure as well as in its renewal procedure. You choose the validity during the application.

extraFaqs.q: How long does it take to get the card?
extraFaqs.a: FRSC's published standard is a temporary licence issued on the spot at capture with 60 days of validity, and the permanent card collected from the State BIR or MVAA after 60 days. FRSC's service agreement also says the reason must be communicated back to the applicant if the permanent card will not be ready inside that standard.

extraFaqs.q: My licence expired more than six months ago. Can I still renew?
extraFaqs.a: FRSC requires a driving test if six months have elapsed since you last held a valid licence. Everything else about the renewal stays the same.

extraFaqs.q: How much is driving school in Nigeria?
extraFaqs.a: We could not verify a national figure, so we are not going to quote one. Driving school charges are set by each school and are not published on a national FRSC page. Get the full cost in writing from a certified school before you enrol.

extraFaqs.q: Is the licence fee different in different states?
extraFaqs.a: FRSC's harmonisation documents state that the licence fee is the same across the country. What differs is what you pay a driving school, and what state agencies charge for the learner's permit and the driving test.

extraFaqs.q: How do I check that a driving school is properly certified?
extraFaqs.a: Search the school by state on the FRSC Driving School Standardisation Programme portal at dssp.frsc.gov.ng. FRSC grades certified schools from A (90–100% in the assessment) to E (50–59%), and a school scoring below 50% is not certified at all. Instructors are certified by FRSC too and renew annually. Ask for the school's grade and its instructors' details before you pay.

extraFaqs.q: Can I verify a driver's licence myself, including from abroad?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. FRSC runs the verification at ndlverification.frsc.gov.ng: sign up, upload an application letter plus the front and back of the licence and any means of ID, add shipping details if you want the extract posted, and pay the verification and shipping fees by debit card. FRSC's service agreement states the extract should be ready within 10 working days, and shipped documents carry a tracking number you confirm on the portal.

extraFaqs.q: Is there a digital driver's licence (eNDL)?
extraFaqs.a: Yes, and the portal's notice sets the rules. Fresh applicants are required to complete the full application process including biometric enrolment before activating it, and an expired licence has to be renewed first. The eNDL app is currently Android-only. Someone offering to 'activate your eNDL' without the biometric steps is describing a card that will not verify.

extraFaqs.q: The portal shows a licence fee that is not the ₦10,350 or ₦15,450 on this page. Which is right?
extraFaqs.a: Pay the amount the portal's own payment page generates against its reference. We could not verify any newer published fee on an FRSC page when we last checked on 14 October 2026, so we will not print a guess. What we can tell you is what not to do: never pay cash to a person who cannot show you the reference on the portal.

extraFaqs.q: How do I track my application without paying an agent?
extraFaqs.a: Use the portal's own tools: track application status with your application id or licence number and date of birth, print the application form, print the acknowledgement slip, and edit the application if you spot a mistake before capture. Keep every reference. An agent adds nothing at this stage except a fee.

extraFaqs.q: Do I really have to complete 26 sessions at a driving school?
extraFaqs.a: For a fresh private licence, yes — FRSC's service agreement puts the training at 26 sessions with the school's exam and capture, and the certificate number is what calls up your record on the portal. The only documented bypass we could verify is the foreign-licence reciprocity route, where the DSSP portal approves the record and generates a unique identity number for holders of a foreign licence. Renewals skip driving school entirely.

extraTakeaways: Fresh licence: 18 or older, learner's permit, certified driving school, VIO test, online application, payment, BIR or MVAA confirmation, biometric capture at the DLC.
Renewal: apply within one calendar month before expiry. No driving school and no VIO test, unless six months have passed since your licence lapsed.
Temporary licence is issued on the spot and is valid for 60 days. The permanent card comes from the State BIR or MVAA after 60 days.
The only fee we could verify on an FRSC page is ₦10,350 for three years or ₦15,450 for five years. Confirm the current amount in the portal.
If nobody captured your biometrics at an FRSC centre, the card is not real.
FRSC grades driving schools from A (90–100% in the assessment) down to E (50–59%); a school scoring below 50% is not certified at all, and its certificate should not be carrying your application.

You can verify a licence yourself at ndlverification.frsc.gov.ng — sign up, upload an application letter plus both sides of the licence and any means of ID, pay by debit card, and FRSC's service agreement says the extract should be ready within 10 working days.

docs.title: Prepaid Electricity Bands (Band A–E): What ₦10,000 of Units Buys in 2026
docs.short: Your NERC service band sets how many hours of supply your feeder should give you, and your DisCo sets what you pay for each unit (kWh). Neither number is national: NERC approves a separate rate for each DisCo, every month.
docs.fee: No single national rate — NERC approves rates per DisCo and per band. In the two September 2026 orders we read, Band A sits at ₦209.50 per kWh for both Eko (EKEDP) and Benin (BEDC), while Band B is ₦61.00 for Eko and ₦68.56 for Benin.
docs.feeSource: Read directly from NERC's September 2026 supplementary orders for Eko Electricity Distribution Plc (Order/NERC/2026/091) and Benin Electricity Distribution Company (Order/NERC/2026/089), both effective 1 September 2026. Your own DisCo's rate is in its own order on nerc.gov.ng.
docs.timeline: Rates are re-set monthly through NERC supplementary orders, so they can move with little notice. NERC requires your DisCo to tell you about rate reviews on your bill or through its other channels.
steps: Find your meter number and your account or MRDN number on your last vending receipt or bill.
Read two numbers off the receipt: the amount you paid and the units (kWh) credited.
Divide the amount by the units, then take off VAT. NERC's own tariff FAQ says that gives you your effective rate.
Compare that rate with the approved rows for your DisCo in its latest NERC supplementary order on nerc.gov.ng.
Check your DisCo's published feeder band list, or its daily rolling seven-day average supply hours for Band A feeders, to see which band your feeder is on.
Keep three months of receipts side by side. Units per day tells you far more than the naira amount you spent.
If your supply falls short of your band, write a formal letter to the DisCo and copy NERC. NERC's FAQ says the DisCo's performance is evaluated over 60 days before rates are adjusted.
documents: Your last three vending receipts (paper, SMS or e-receipt)
Your DisCo account or MRDN number
The name of your feeder or estate, if you are disputing your band
Screenshots or photos of your DisCo's published supply hours, if you are complaining
A clear photo of the meter and its seal, if you suspect a fault
pitfalls: Assuming there is one national tariff. There is not. NERC approves rates for each DisCo, and the lower bands differ widely between them.
Comparing your unit cost with a friend's in another DisCo, or in another band.
Working out your rate from a receipt without taking VAT and any fixed monthly charge off first.
Paying anyone to move you to a better band. Migration is decided by NERC from measured feeder performance, not by payment.
Buying a prepaid meter from an unauthorised seller instead of through the DisCo or an approved vendor.
Leaving a suspected faulty meter unreported for months and then trying to argue the bill.
Reading a blog's 'national electricity tariff' table as if it applied to your own feeder.
docs.metaTitle: Prepaid Electricity Bands Band A–E: NERC Tariff & What ₦10,000 Buys
docs.metaDescription: How NERC bands A to E set your hours of supply, why your kWh rate differs by DisCo, verified ₦/kWh rows from two September 2026 NERC orders, and how to work out your own rate from a vending receipt.

how many units is 10000 naira of prepaid electricity

headings.cost: How to check the cost before you pay

docs.sourceNote: Band definitions, the 60-day failure review and the receipt method are from NERC's own Electricity Tariffs FAQ. The naira-per-kWh rows are read directly from two NERC September 2026 supplementary orders — Order/NERC/2026/091 for Eko Electricity Distribution Plc and Order/NERC/2026/089 for Benin Electricity Distribution Company — both effective 1 September 2026. This page is checked by hand and is not an automatically updated feed.

officialLinks.label: NERC — Electricity Tariffs FAQ (service bands A to E)
NERC — September 2026 supplementary order for Eko Electricity Distribution Plc (PDF)
NERC — September 2026 supplementary order for Benin Electricity Distribution Company (PDF)
NERC — resources library (orders, MYTO and monthly energy caps)

unverifiedItems: The current rate for your own DisCo. We verified Eko (EKEDP) and Benin (BEDC) only, and only for the yet-to-be-transitioned states inside each franchise. Open your DisCo's latest supplementary order on nerc.gov.ng.
Rates in states that have moved to their own state electricity regulator. Those are approved by the state regulator, not by the NERC orders quoted here.
The fixed monthly service charge, meter maintenance charge and VAT treatment on your specific account. Your vending receipt is the authority.
Which band your own feeder sits on today. Bands are reviewed monthly and feeders are upgraded and downgraded by NERC order.
extraIntro: Band A means NERC's service promise of a minimum of 20 hours of supply a day. Band B is 16 hours, Band C 12, Band D 8 and Band E 4. That is the definition NERC publishes in its own electricity tariff FAQ, and it is the reason Band A costs the most per unit.

What complicates everything is that your rate is not national. NERC issues a supplementary order for each DisCo every month, and each order carries its own table. We read two of them — Eko (EKEDP) and Benin (BEDC), both effective 1 September 2026 — and the two tables already disagree on Bands B to E. This page reflects what we verified on 12 October 2026 and is not an automatically updated feed.

extraSections.h2: What the five service bands actually mean
paras: NERC introduced the Service-Based Tariff to tie what you pay to the service you actually receive. It took effect on 1 November 2020. It groups every feeder into one of five bands, measured by the average hours of supply per day over one month.

Your band is a property of your feeder, not a choice you make, and it can change. NERC reviews feeder performance monthly and issues orders that upgrade or downgrade feeders, so an estate can move in either direction.
The five bands, exactly as NERC states them in its electricity tariff FAQ:

table.caption: NERC service bands and the minimum daily supply each one commits to. Source: NERC Electricity Tariffs FAQ, read on 12 October 2026.
columns: Minimum hours of supply per day
rows: The highest committed service level, and the highest rate per unit.
Most of the day, with gaps. Noticeably cheaper per unit than Band A.
About half the day. Many urban and peri-urban feeders sit here.
Supply in blocks rather than continuously.
The lowest committed service level under the scheme.

extraSections.h2: What one unit costs, and why nobody can quote you one national figure
paras: There is no single 'Nigeria electricity tariff'. NERC approves an end-user rate for each DisCo, and the bands below Band A are not uniform across the country either.

The table below is taken from two NERC supplementary orders that took effect on 1 September 2026. Both approve rates for the 'yet to be transitioned states' inside each DisCo's franchise area — Ogun State for Eko (EKEDP), and Edo plus Delta for Benin (BEDC). If you live in a state that has moved its electricity regulation to a state regulator, your rate is approved by that state regulator, not by these orders.
Notice that Band A is the same in both tables and the lower bands are not. That is the clearest illustration of why a friend's unit cost in another state tells you nothing about yours.
Non-MD means customers on a single or three-phase connection, which is what most homes and small shops are. MD customers are on maximum-demand connections and have their own rows in the same orders.

table.caption: Approved end-user rates in naira per kWh, in force from 1 September 2026 — NERC September 2026 supplementary orders for Eko (Order/NERC/2026/091) and Benin (Order/NERC/2026/089).
rows: Lifeline (R1, up to 50 kWh a month)

extraSections.h2: What ₦10,000 of units actually buys
paras: One unit is one kilowatt-hour (kWh). It is what a 1,000-watt appliance uses in one hour, or what a 100-watt bulb uses in ten hours. To estimate what an appliance costs you, take the watt rating on its nameplate, divide by 1,000, and multiply by the hours you run it.

Using the Eko (EKEDP) rows above, here is the straight-line answer to the question people actually ask. Divide ₦10,000 by the rate and you get the units — before VAT and before any fixed monthly charge come off, which is why a real receipt always shows fewer units than this.

Put another way: the same ₦10,000 buys roughly three times more electricity on a Band B feeder than on a Band A feeder, and about six times more on Band E. That gap is the whole argument behind the band system, and it is why the first question to ask before comparing bills is which band the other person is on.

table.caption: Straight-line estimate using the Eko (EKEDP) non-MD rates approved from 1 September 2026. VAT and fixed charges reduce the units on a real receipt.

extraSections.h2: How to work out your own rate from a receipt
paras: You do not need a blog table. NERC's own tariff FAQ answers this directly: divide the amount you vended by the number of kWh units shown on the receipt, and deduct the VAT. The result is your effective rate.
Do it across three months. Units per day is the figure that actually tells you whether your consumption moved or your rate did.
bullets: ₦10,000 that credits 45 units works out at about ₦222 per unit before VAT — close to the Band A row.
If your worked-out rate does not match any row in your DisCo's order, query it with the DisCo before assuming the meter is fine.
Keep the receipts. A photo of each one on your phone is enough, and it is your evidence if you ever need to dispute a charge.

extraSections.h2: Grid, generator or solar: how to compare them properly
paras: Band A supply is expensive per unit, but it is often still cheaper per hour than running a generator. The only honest way to settle it for your own home is to put your real numbers in, which is what the two power calculators on this site are for.

Run the generator calculator with your actual load in kilowatts and your real running hours to get a daily and monthly fuel figure. Then put that monthly figure into the solar payback calculator together with the system cost you have been quoted.
bullets: Generator calculator: turns load, hours and the fuel price into a monthly bill.
Solar payback calculator: divides the system cost by what you would save each year.
Both calculators run in your browser and both state the assumptions they use.

extraSections.h2: If your light does not match your band
paras: NERC's tariff FAQ sets out what should happen when a DisCo fails to deliver the minimum hours for a band. The DisCo's performance is evaluated over 60 days, and once the Commission verifies the failure, the rates for every customer in that cluster are adjusted to match the service actually delivered.

NERC also requires each DisCo to publish a rolling seven-day average of daily supply hours for every Band A feeder on its own website each day, and to explain publicly any two-day failure. That publication is your evidence.

Start with a formal letter to the DisCo describing the shortfall and copy NERC. NERC's FAQ asks communities that want a better band to write formally and to copy the Commission so it can help facilitate the request.

extraFaqs.q: Is there one Band A tariff for the whole of Nigeria?
extraFaqs.a: No. NERC approves end-user rates for each DisCo separately, and the orders it issues each month carry their own tables. The two September 2026 orders we read both put Band A at ₦209.50 per kWh, but their Bands B to E rows differ. States that have moved to their own electricity regulator approve their own rates.

extraFaqs.q: How do I find out which band my feeder is on?
extraFaqs.a: Your tariff class is printed on your bill or your vending receipt. For the band itself, check your DisCo's published feeder list and its daily rolling seven-day average supply hours, which NERC requires it to publish for every Band A feeder.

extraFaqs.q: Why did my ₦10,000 finish faster this month?
extraFaqs.a: Compare units, not naira. Count the days the credit lasted and the units per day. A rate change, a new appliance, a longer month, a meter fault and a fixed monthly charge all show up differently, and only the units tell you which one it was.

extraFaqs.q: Can I pay to be moved to Band A?
extraFaqs.a: No. Migration between bands follows NERC's review of measured feeder performance, and NERC issues the order. Anyone who asks you for money to upgrade your meter or your band is selling you nothing.

extraFaqs.q: What is a lifeline customer?
extraFaqs.a: NERC's R1 lifeline class covers customers whose consumption is not more than 50 kWh a month. In the two orders we read, the lifeline rate is ₦4.00 per kWh.

extraFaqs.q: Does VAT come out of my vending?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. NERC's own tariff FAQ tells customers to deduct VAT before working out the rate implied by a vending receipt.

extraFaqs.q: Is Band A supply cheaper than running my generator?
extraFaqs.a: Often, but it depends entirely on your load and your hours. Put your real numbers into the generator fuel calculator, then compare the monthly figure with what you spend on units.

extraFaqs.q: Do these rates apply to me if I live in Lagos or another state with its own electricity regulator?
extraFaqs.a: The NERC orders quoted here approve rates for the yet-to-be-transitioned states inside each DisCo's franchise. If your state has transferred regulatory oversight to a state electricity regulator, that regulator approves your rate. Check with your DisCo and with your state regulator.

extraTakeaways: Band A promises a minimum of 20 hours of supply a day; Band B 16, Band C 12, Band D 8 and Band E 4. That is NERC's own definition.
Your rate is per DisCo, not national. The two September 2026 orders we read agree on Band A at ₦209.50 per kWh and disagree on Bands B to E.
At that Band A rate, ₦10,000 is roughly 48 units before VAT and fixed charges. On Band B it is roughly 164 units.
Work out your own rate from a receipt: amount divided by units, less VAT. NERC says so itself.
Nobody can sell you a band upgrade, and nobody should sell you a meter outside the DisCo or approved-vendor process.

docs.title: Lagos State Residency Registration (LASRRA / LAG-ID): Documents, Centres and Card Collection
docs.short: Registering with LASRRA is free — ₦0 for the registration and for your first residency card, according to the agency's own registration FAQ, which we read on 12 October 2026. You take one proof of the Lagos address where you actually live and one photo ID from the agency's list, get a temporary registration card on the spot, and collect the permanent LAG-ID card from your LG or LCDA when LASRRA tells you it is ready.
docs.fee: ₦0 — nothing. LASRRA's registration FAQ says the residency card is produced and issued free of charge to all residents and that there is no cost to register. There is no fee table for LASRRA because there is no fee.
docs.feeSource: LASRRA registration FAQ, “How much does the Residency Card Cost?”, on the official portal at registration.lagosresidents.gov.ng/help/faq, read on 12 October 2026. The agency's 2026 sensitisation messages repeat that registration is free and warn against anyone collecting money for it.
docs.timeline: A temporary registration card is issued at the centre once your fingerprints, signature and face image are captured, and LASRRA's FAQ says it is valid for 12 months. The same FAQ says the permanent residency card is printed within 12 months of registration and delivered to the LG or LCDA of the address you registered, where you collect it after an SMS notification. Records with errors go on hold, and the agency says that can take over five weeks to resolve.
steps: Check that you qualify. LASRRA's FAQ says anyone who currently resides in the state is required to register, and so is anyone taking up residence who intends to stay more than six months.

Make sure you can prove the Lagos address where you actually live. The FAQ is direct about this: to be eligible, you must be able to provide a valid and verifiable address. No address document, no registration.

Assemble the two-part document set: one proof of residence (rent receipt or tenancy agreement, or a utility bill for the address such as electricity, water or refuse disposal) and one proof of identity from the agency's list (international passport, national ID card, driver's licence, employee ID card carrying the employer's address or logo, student ID card, tax card or receipt, association ID, or a letter of identification from a parent, CDA, household head or registered association).
Bring originals and clean photocopies of everything. The portal says the registration officer scans the documents and hands them back, but keeps a copy.

Pre-register online at registration.lagosresidents.gov.ng/register and print the confirmation page. The portal says filling the online form is only step one, and that you must still attend an enrolment station for your biometrics.
If you would rather start at a centre, you can. The FAQ lists two modes of registration: online, or attending a registration point near you.

Find the centre inside your own local government or LCDA on the portal's locator at registration.lagosresidents.gov.ng/help/enrollment. Choose the LG or LCDA where you live, because that is where your permanent card is sent.
Attend with your documents and your printed online confirmation page. The officer captures ten fingerprints, your signature and your face image, and issues your temporary registration card.

Register your children on the same trip if you can. Children aged 15 and under are registered without biometrics; you need the child's birth certificate, two passport-sized photographs of the child, and a copy of the registration card of an adult who has already registered.

Wait for the SMS, then collect the permanent card from the LG or LCDA office named in the message. Keep the temporary card safe in the meantime — it is your evidence of registration until the permanent one arrives.

Validate your record when LASRRA asks you to, or if your name or address has changed. The portal's validation page exists to confirm that the information that will be printed on your card is accurate and reflects your current status.
documents: Proof of residence in Lagos: rent receipt or tenancy agreement, or a utility bill for the address you live at (electricity, water or refuse disposal bill)

One proof of identity: international passport, national ID card, driver's licence, employee ID card showing the employer's address or logo, student ID card, tax card or receipt, association ID, or a letter of identification from a parent, CDA, household head or registered association
Originals plus clean photocopies of each document, because the officer keeps a copy
The printed online confirmation page with your Online Registration Id, if you pre-registered
A phone number you will still be using months later, because that is how the collection SMS reaches you
For a child: the child's birth certificate, two passport photographs of the child, and a photocopy of the registration card of the adult registering the child
For domestic staff: a notarised copy of the employer's utility bill or rent receipt
Evidence of the new address if you are updating a record after moving house
pitfalls: Paying anybody for registration. The card and the registration are free, and the agency has warned residents about agents collecting money for it.
Carrying a utility bill for a different address from the one you are registering. The proof has to match where you actually live.
Assuming a NIN slip is on the identity list. The published list names the National ID card, not the NIN slip. If that is all you hold, ask the centre before you travel.
Treating the temporary registration card as if it were the LAG-ID smart card. The temporary card is paper proof of registration; the chip-based card is the permanent one.
Registering in the LG or LCDA where you work instead of where you live. The permanent card is sent to the address you registered.
Letting a spelling error pass on the officer's screen. Fixing it after the card is printed means handing the card back and waiting 10 to 15 working days.

Losing the card and assuming the replacement is free. The FAQ says the first card is free and later cards may be replaced at a charge; no amount is published, so ask the helpdesk rather than an agent.
Believing a 'concierge' who says he can speed up printing. The delays LASRRA itself describes come from record checks, not from who submits the form.

extraIntro: Two things send people home from a LASRRA centre before they even sit down. The first is the wrong paper: the agency wants proof of where you live in Lagos, and an electricity bill in a landlord's name that you cannot connect to yourself is a problem. The second is paying for something that is free — the registration and the first card cost nothing, and the agency has publicly warned residents about agents collecting money for it.

What changed for many families in 2026 is who needs the number. On 3 September 2026 the Office of Education Quality Assurance announced that schools would obtain and record the valid LASRRA registration number of every learner as part of admission and enrolment from 14 September 2026, for the 2026/2027 session, in both public and private schools.

One warning about sources. The agency's own informational website, www.lagosresidents.gov.ng, was returning a WordPress critical error when we checked on 12 October 2026. The registration portal at registration.lagosresidents.gov.ng was up and working, and every rule on this page comes from there, from Lagos State's own service pages, or from the two agency press items named below. Where something could not be confirmed, we say so instead of filling the gap.

extraSections.h2: Where to register: the centre for your own local government
paras: LASRRA registers through local governments and local council development areas. The portal's centre locator lists 57 LG and LCDA options — from Agbado Oke Odo, Agege and Alimosho through Mushin and Shomolu to Yaba — and shows the centres inside whichever one you choose.

We are not printing a list of street addresses here, and that is deliberate. Centres move, and the agency's own locator is the only list that stays current; a copied address list is exactly the thing that goes stale on old forum threads. Open the locator, pick the LG or LCDA where you live, and go to the centre nearest you.

The FAQ also notes that LASRRA has mobile teams that move from area to area, and the agency's 2026 sensitisation drive is taking registration to schools, markets and other public points. If a team is announced in your area, confirm it with the LASRRA desk in your LG or LCDA before you hand over documents — or money.
bullets: Pre-register online, then attend a centre: the portal describes the online form as step one only, with biometrics still to be captured at an enrolment station.
Walk in and register at a centre instead: the FAQ lists both online and walk-in registration.
Either way, if you started online, print the confirmation page and carry it with your documents.
Register where you live, not where you work. The permanent card is sent to the LG or LCDA of your registered address.

extraSections.h2: What the LAG-ID card is for
paras: The residency number is the state's reference for you, and several Lagos services now hang off it. These are the ones with an official source behind them:

table.caption: Official Lagos State sources, read on 12 October 2026.
rows: Schools are to obtain and record the valid LASRRA registration number of every learner from 14 September 2026, for the 2026/2027 session, in public and private schools — Office of Education Quality Assurance press release, 3 September 2026.

LASHMA deployed biometric card readers integrated with the LASRRA database so that ILERA EKO enrollees are authenticated with their LASRRA ID, starting with a pilot across 100 facilities — Lagos State Ministry of Health, May 2025.
Citizens Gate lists the requirements to apply as LASRRA ID, NIN and a Citizen ID.
Citizens Gate describes LASRRA card holders as having access to BRT, loans and other financial benefits.

bullets: It is not a travel document. The portal's FAQ leaves the answer to that question blank, so treat the card as domestic proof of residency.
It does not make you an indigene of Lagos State. The FAQ is clear that registration confers no status other than that you resided in the state when you registered.

It is not a replacement for your NIN or your voter's card. Different agencies collect different records, and the FAQ says the national identity database is a separate entity from the Lagos State residents register.

extraSections.h2: Temporary registration card vs the permanent LAG-ID card
paras: Half the confusion at the counter is that two different things are called 'the card'. Only one of them is the LAG-ID.

That you have registered and your record is in the system
Your proof of residency, with your residency number printed on it
Handed to you at the centre
An SMS tells you it is ready; you collect it at the LG or LCDA of your registered address
Chip-based and multifunction: the Ministry of Health describes it as enabling access to healthcare, payments and identity verification

extraSections.h2: How to check where your card is
paras: Start with the portal's validation page. Its stated purpose is to confirm that the information that will be printed on your card is accurate and reflects your current status, and it lets you start a validation or retrieve one you saved earlier.
Lagos State's own website lists a 'Check LAG-ID Status' service under Identity Management, next to LASRRA registration, at lagosstate.gov.ng/services/identitymanagement.

The short code that LASRRA officers and the agency's social posts have handed out for checking card status is *347*641#, sometimes written *347641#. We could not find it written on a live agency page on 12 October 2026, so treat it as something to confirm with the LASRRA desk. Send it from the phone number you registered with, and never send money afterwards to anybody who claims to be following it up.

extraSections.h2: Delays, and what LASRRA itself says about them
paras: LASRRA's FAQ is unusually blunt about the gap between capture and collection. After registration comes a quality check, then corrections where needed, then screening, validation and de-duplication — only after that is your residency number generated. If an error is found, the record is put on hold for enquiry, the applicant is contacted using the contact details given, and the agency says resolution can take over five weeks.
That is the honest timeline. Nothing you pay an agent changes it, and the printing order is not something a 'fast track' fee controls.
bullets: Details that do not match your documents are the commonest cause of a hold. Watch the officer's screen and correct spellings on the spot.
An error found after printing: the card is taken back for amendment and LASRRA says replacement cards are ready in 10 to 15 working days.
A move within Lagos: you do not re-register. The FAQ says you inform the nearest registration station with evidence of the new address and your record is updated.
Hospital admission: if you are on admission when your turn comes, the FAQ exempts you until discharge and says the team will not visit the hospital to register people.

Lost or stolen card: report it promptly to the nearest registration office or the LASRRA headquarters helpdesk. The first card is free; the FAQ says subsequent cards may be replaced at a charge, and no amount is published — ask the desk first.

extraFaqs.q: Is LASRRA registration really free?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. LASRRA's registration FAQ says the residency card is produced and issued free of charge to all residents and that there is no cost to register. That is why there is no fee table on this page — there is no fee to publish. The agency has repeatedly warned residents about agents collecting money for registration, so if anybody asks you for a capture charge or a payment to speed up your card, note who it was and report it to the LASRRA desk or through Lagos State Citizens Gate.

extraFaqs.q: Do I need a NIN to register?
extraFaqs.a: The published document list asks for proof of your Lagos address plus one photo ID, and the National ID card is one of the accepted IDs. A NIN slip is not named on that list, so if the NIN slip is the only identity paper you hold, ask the centre before you travel. Where a NIN is definitely required is downstream: Lagos State Citizens Gate lists LASRRA ID, NIN and a Citizen ID as the requirements for state financial assistance. Never pay an agent to 'link' your NIN to anything.

extraFaqs.q: Can non-indigenes and foreign nationals register?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. The FAQ says registration is open to everyone irrespective of age, race, ethnic origin, religious affiliation or nationality, so long as the person currently resides in Lagos State. Domestic staff living in your household are covered whatever their nationality: a notarised rent receipt or utility bill of the employer serves as the address evidence, and the employer can register them at the same time as their own registration. What the card does not do is confer indigene status.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between the temporary slip and the LAG-ID card?
extraFaqs.a: The temporary registration card is issued at the centre and is valid for 12 months. The permanent LAG-ID is the chip-based card, printed after LASRRA's checks and collected from the LG or LCDA where you registered once the SMS arrives. It is the permanent card and the residency number behind it that are used for things like ILERA EKO authentication at the hospital.

extraFaqs.q: How long before my card is ready?
extraFaqs.a: LASRRA's FAQ gives 12 months as the outer limit for printing the permanent card, with delivery to the LG or LCDA of your registered address, and the temporary card covers you for that period. Records with errors go on hold and the agency says that can take over five weeks to resolve. Keep the temporary card safe — it is your evidence of registration while you wait.

extraFaqs.q: I lost my card. What do I do?
extraFaqs.a: Report the loss to the nearest registration office or the LASRRA headquarters helpdesk; the FAQ says lost and stolen cards must be reported promptly, while the first residency card is free and subsequent cards may be replaced at a charge. No amount is published, so ask the desk for the current charge and pay it at the office — not to somebody who meets you at the gate.

extraFaqs.q: Do I need a LASRRA number for my child's school admission?
extraFaqs.a: From the 2026/2027 session, yes. The Office of Education Quality Assurance announced on 3 September 2026 that schools would obtain and record the valid LASRRA registration number of every learner as part of admission and enrolment from 14 September 2026, in both public and private schools. Children aged 15 and under are registered without biometrics, using the child's birth certificate, two passport photographs of the child, and the registration card of an adult who has already registered.

extraFaqs.q: Can somebody else register a child or a house help?
extraFaqs.a: Yes, with the right papers. An adult can register a child aged 15 or under, though the adult must have completed their own registration first, and the FAQ gives the minimum age of that adult as 18 in one answer and over 21 in another, so confirm at the centre if it matters. An employer can help domestic staff who live in the household by providing a notarised copy of the household utility bill or rent receipt, or by bringing them along during the employer's own registration.

extraFaqs.q: What if my card carries a spelling mistake?
extraFaqs.a: Point it out while you are at the centre and can still see the data entry on screen. If you only notice after the permanent card is printed, take it back to the registration officer at the point of collection; the card is collected for amendment and the agency says replacement cards are ready in 10 to 15 working days.

extraFaqs.q: Do I have to validate after registering?
extraFaqs.a: The portal runs a validation exercise, and its own wording is that validation confirms the information that will be printed on your card is accurate and reflects your current status. If you have changed your name or moved house, that is the moment to fix it. The agency is reported to expect revalidation about every five years, but we could not confirm that wording on a live agency page on 12 October 2026, so confirm the timing with your LG or LCDA office.

extraTakeaways: Registration is free: ₦0 for the registration and ₦0 for the first card. Anybody charging you for a LASRRA form, a 'capture fee' or a 'fast card' is charging you for nothing.

Two documents at the centre: proof of the Lagos address where you live (rent receipt, tenancy agreement, electricity, water or refuse bill) plus one photo ID from LASRRA's list, originals and photocopies.
Temporary registration card: printed at the centre, valid 12 months. Permanent LAG-ID card: printed within 12 months, collected from your LG or LCDA after the SMS.
The school angle is now real: from 14 September 2026, Lagos schools record learners' LASRRA numbers for the 2026/2027 session.
Register in the LG or LCDA where you live, not where you work — that is where the card is sent to.
